# Appeal of Denial — Total Ankle Replacement (CPT 27702)

**Governing Policy:** Cigna Medical Coverage Policy 0285 Total Ankle Arthroplasty
https://static.cigna.com/assets/chcp/pdf/coveragePolicies/medical/mm_0285_coveragepositioncriteria_total_ankle_arthroplasty.pdf

**RE: Appeal of Adverse Benefit Determination**
- Member: Sawyer Alvarez
- Member ID: W635441117
- Denial date: 2026-08-11
- Reference number: POC-A1F3D3C000-86797
- Payer/Plan: Cigna, Commercial/ACA, Ohio
- Requested service: Total ankle replacement, CPT 27702

Dear Cigna Appeals Department,

I am appealing the denial of my total ankle replacement, which was denied as not medically necessary in the notice dated 2026-08-11 (reference number POC-A1F3D3C000-86797). My surgeon, Dr. Duval, has documented that this surgery is medically necessary for my condition, and I am asking that the plan reconsider its decision based on Cigna's own coverage policy and the records already in my file.

## The plan's own policy sets out the criteria for my situation

My request is for a **primary** total ankle replacement, not a revision surgery. I want to make sure the review focuses on the correct part of Cigna's policy, because some of the policy's language applies only to revision surgery — a different situation from mine, since I have not had a prior ankle implant.

The policy provisions about implant failure — for example, that "ankle arthroplasty is considered medically necessary for moderate to severe ankle pain secondary to failure of an implanted device (e.g., implant loosening, malpositioning, periprosthetic infection, periprosthetic fracture)" and that "Revision total ankle arthroplasty for any other indication is considered not medically necessary" — describe revision surgery after a prior implant has failed. That is not my case, since I have not had a previous ankle replacement.

The part of the policy that applies to my situation is the standard for a new device as an alternative to fusion surgery. Cigna's policy states that a "Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- approved/cleared device* is considered medically necessary as an alternative to ankle arthrodesis when ALL of the following criteria have been met:" and lists these requirements:

> " is function-limiting at short distances (e.g., walking less than ¼ mile, limiting activity to two city blocks, the equivalent to walking the length of a shopping mall) for at least three (3) months duration  interferes with the ability to carry out age appropriate activities of daily living and/or demands of employment • failure of at least six months of conservative therapy (i.e., anti-inflammatory medications, orthotic devices, activity modification, physical therapy) • individual has NONE of the following contraindications to total ankle arthroplasty:"

My medical records show the following against these requirements:

**Function-limiting for at least three months:** My records document 12 months of progressive ankle pain and that I "ambulate[] with an antalgic gait, limited to two blocks." This matches the policy's own example of "limiting activity to two city blocks" and lasts far longer than the three-month minimum in the policy.

**Failure of at least six months of conservative therapy:** My records show I used NSAIDs for 8 months with inadequate relief, completed 18 visits of supervised physical therapy over 10 weeks (2026-04-18 to 2026-06-27) per the physical therapy discharge note, and received a corticosteroid injection on 2026-04-29 that gave only 2 weeks of partial relief. These are the same categories of conservative care the policy lists — "anti-inflammatory medications... and physical therapy" — and the medication trial alone exceeds the policy's six-month threshold.

**Interference with daily activities or work:** My chart documents that I walk with an antalgic gait limited to two blocks, which reflects meaningful functional limitation. I recognize the citations provided to me do not include a separate, specific statement in my chart addressing employment or activities of daily living beyond this functional description, and I am not asking the plan to assume facts not in my records. If Cigna needs additional documentation on this point specifically, I ask that the plan identify what is missing so my surgeon's office can supply it.

**Absence of contraindications:** My records note no active infection and no untreated substance use. The specific list of contraindications referenced in the policy was not included in the materials available to me for this letter, so I cannot confirm point-by-point that every listed contraindication is addressed, but nothing in my chart indicates any of the concerns typically associated with this surgery.

I also want to point out that my imaging and exam findings are consistent with the severity of arthritis the policy contemplates before surgery is considered. My weight-bearing ankle radiographs from 2026-06-02 show "tibiotalar joint space obliteration with subchondral cysts," and my exam showed "positive provocative testing on the affected side" with "range of motion limited by pain." Total ankle arthroplasty/replacement for any other indication is considered not medically necessary.

0285 Revision total ankle arthroplasty is considered medically necessary for moderate to severe ankle pain secondary to failure of an implanted device (e.g., implant loosening, malpositioning, periprosthetic infection, periprosthetic fracture).

Conservative management typically consists of medications for pain control, limiting activity, the use of ankle braces to stabilize the joint, shoe modifications, heat, and physical therapy to control the pain associated with ankle arthrosis.
When conservative management fails, ankle arthrodesis (AA) (fusion) has been the standard surgical treatment of choice to control the pain of severe ankle arthritis.
Revision Surgery Revision surgery may be necessary in the presence of failed arthroplasty.
Failed arthroplasty is typically suspected when pain occurs progressively over time and is persistent, indicating implant loosening and collapse.
Surgical management of failed TAR may include ankle arthrodesi s, revision arthroplasty, or amputation.
Treatment of early talar AVN may include conservative measures like non- or protective weightbearing, or joint-sparing procedures (e.g., core decompression, bone grafting).
evidence.submission_route: Log in at my.cigna.com to find your plan's appeal form and submit it there, or call the number on your card. The mailing address is plan-specific — use the one on your denial letter. Online: my.cigna.com By phone: 1-800-244-6224, or the number on your card Deadline: Usually 180 days from the denial -- but your denial letter is authoritative.
